    Nine of the remaining sons of Ṛṣabhadeva became the rulers of the nine islands of Bhārata-varṣa, and they exercised complete sovereignty over this planet. Eighty-one sons became twice-born brāhmaṇas and helped initiate the Vedic path of fruitive sacrifices [karma-kāṇḍa].
    Purport

    The nine dvīpas, or islands, ruled by nine sons of Ṛṣabhadeva are the nine varṣas of Jambudvīpa, namely Bhārata, Kinnara, Hari, Kuru, Hiraṇmaya, Ramyaka, Ilāvṛta, Bhadrāśva and Ketumāla.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Nine of the remaining sons of Ṛṣabhadeva became the rulers of the nine islands of Bhārata-varṣa and they exercised complete sovereignty over this planet. Eighty-one sons became brāhmaṇas and helped initiate the Vedic path of karma. Among the sons of Ṛṣabha, nine became rulers of nine islands such as Brahmāvarta within Bhārata-varṣa. Eighty-one sons became brāhmaṇas who started the path of karma.
    Personal Guidance
    Sovereignty and brāhmaṇical learning are both legitimate services within varṇāśrama — divisions of labor in Kṛṣṇa's order, not personal kingdoms.
    Practical Applications
    • Locate the small 'dvīpa' you actually govern today — your desk, your team, your home — and rule it as a steward under Kṛṣṇa, not as its owner.
    • Notice when you envy another's role and remind yourself that ruler and brāhmaṇa are complementary services, not rungs on a ladder.
    • Refuse to flatten varṇāśrama into modern egalitarian sameness; honor the specific duty that has landed in your hands this week.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which 'island' of responsibility have I quietly been treating as my private domain rather than as a service entrusted to me?
    • Where am I confusing the karma-kāṇḍa work I am called to do with the ultimate goal, forgetting that even Vedic sacrifice points beyond itself?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Treat your hostel room, study group, or first internship desk as a small dvīpa you govern as a steward — keep it clean, fair, and offered to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Notice when social media nudges you to envy a friend's 'role' (popular leader vs. quiet topper) and remind yourself both are services, not rankings.
    • Refuse the campus story that ambition and learning are opposed; do your assigned coursework as karma-kāṇḍa-like regulated duty, with Kṛṣṇa as the eventual aim.
    householder
    • Map your household as your dvīpa — spouse, children, finances, parents — and rule it under Kṛṣṇa, not as its proprietor.
    • When career envy arises between you and a peer (the 'ruler' executive vs. the 'brāhmaṇa' teacher), name it as forgetting that both are sva-dharma posts.
    • Use your earning and ritual life (festivals, ekādaśī, family worship) as regulated karma that gradually turns the home toward bhakti, not as ends in themselves.
    senior
    • Hand over the 'island' you once ruled — business, household, institution — deliberately, training successors as Ṛṣabhadeva's sons were trained for distinct roles.
    • Mentor younger householders to see their duties as service-posts under Kṛṣṇa, not as identities they must cling to.
    • Let the karma-kāṇḍa phase of life loosen its grip: keep regulated duties, but turn the remaining years increasingly toward direct surrender to Kṛṣṇa.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the nine rulers and eighty-one brāhmaṇas as a hierarchy of worth instead of a division of function.
    • Romanticizing the brāhmaṇa role and despising one's actual kṣatriya- or vaiśya-like duties as 'lower'.
    • Mistaking karma-kāṇḍa ritual competence for the goal of life, forgetting that fruitive sacrifice is only a preparatory stage.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one concrete way varṇāśrama could shape a decision you face this month — and where you suspect the group will disagree with you.
    • Is it healthier for a modern student to identify with the nine rulers or the eighty-one brāhmaṇas of this verse? Defend your answer against the opposite view.
    • Where does the karma-kāṇḍa path help a sincere seeker, and where does it become a trap that delays surrender to Kṛṣṇa?
    Role Play

    Two classmates: one has just been promoted to manage a small team (a 'ruler' of a tiny dvīpa); the other has been asked to teach a weekly scripture class (a 'brāhmaṇa' role). Each privately envies the other. Stage a five-minute conversation in which they help one another see their post as service under Kṛṣṇa rather than as identity or rank.

    Objections & Responses
    • Dividing humanity into rulers and brāhmaṇas sounds like a caste system used to oppress people — why preserve it?
      Varṇāśrama as Kṛṣṇa intends it is a division of natural propensity and service, not of birth-based oppression; the verse shows sons of one father taking different functions, all in service to dharma. The abuse of the system is not the system; recovering its real shape protects, rather than crushes, the individual.
    • Karma-kāṇḍa sacrifices feel like primitive ritualism — what relevance do eighty-one brāhmaṇas initiating fruitive sacrifices have for me?
      Karma-kāṇḍa is a graded ladder: it trains a materially-minded person in regulated action, gradually purifying desire until bhakti can take root. The verse is not asking you to revive fire sacrifices; it is asking you to honor regulated duty as the proper soil from which surrender to Kṛṣṇa eventually grows.

    The nine remaining sons of Ṛṣabha were greatly fortunate sages who worked vigorously to spread knowledge of the Absolute Truth. They wandered about naked and were very well versed in spiritual science. Their names were Kavi, Havir, Antarīkṣa, Prabuddha, Pippalāyana, Āvirhotra, Drumila, Camasa and Karabhājana.
    Purport

    Nimi, the King of Videha, asked the following nine questions of the nine Yogendras, the saintly sons of Ṛṣabha. (1) What is the highest good? (Chapter Two, verse 30); (2) What are the religious principles ( dharma ), natural proclivities ( svabhāva ), behavior ( ācāra ), speech ( vākya ) and outward symptoms ( lakṣaṇa ) of a bhāgavata, a Vaiṣṇava devotee of the Lord? (2.44); (3) What is the external energy of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord? (3.1); (4) How can one become dissociated from this māyā ? (3.17); (5)What is the true identity of Brahman? (3.34); (6) What are the three types of karma, namely karma based on the enjoyment of the fruits of work, karma offered to the Supreme Lord, and naiṣkarmya ? (3.41); (7) What are the various pastimes of the various incarnations of God? (4.1); (8) What is the aim or destination of one who is against the Supreme Lord and devoid of bhakti (in other words, a nondevotee)? (5.1); and (9)What are the respective colors, forms and names of the four yugāvatāras, the four incarnations of the Supreme Lord who appear in the four ages, and what is the process of worshiping each of Them? (5.19).

    The transcendental answers to these inquiries were given by the great devotees Kavi, Havir, Antarīkṣa, Prabuddha, Pippalāyana, Āvirhotra, Drumila, Camasa and Karabhājana. These nine paramahaṁsas answered the nine questions, each in turn, in the following verses: (1) 2.33-43; (2) 2.45-55; (3) 3.3-16; (4) 3.18-33; (5) 3.35-40; (6) 3.43-55; (7) 4.2-23; (8) 5.2-18; and (9) 5.20-42.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The nine remaining sons of Ṛṣabha, greatly fortunate sages, discerning the highest truth and endeavoring for Paramātmā, were learned concerning Paramātmā. They wandered about naked. Their names were Kavi, Havir, Antarīkṣa, Prabuddha, Pippalāyana, Āvirhotra, Drumila, Camasa and Karabhājana. They were discerners of the highest truth (artha-śaṁsinaḥ), making great endeavor for realizing ātmā, and were naked (vāta-rasanā).

    • RGS SB 11-02-21-33 Hindi - Nimi Navyogendra Samvad-03 - Vrindavan
      His Holiness Radha Govinda Swami· English
    Personal Guidance
    The nine Yogendras — naked, wandering sages versed in ātma-vidyā — exist to answer Nimi's real questions about bhakti; receive their teaching as living transmission, not lore.
    Practical Applications
    • Write down the one question about Kṛṣṇa-bhakti you have been avoiding asking aloud, and bring it to a sādhu, a verse, or your guru today.
    • Refuse the modern habit of treating spiritual instruction as content; receive today's reading as a personal answer from a paramahaṁsa to a question you actually carry.
    • Identify one possession or comfort you cling to as 'mine' and, for one day, hold it as the vāta-rasanā Yogendras would — useful, but not your shelter.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which of Nimi's nine questions — about the highest good, māyā, Brahman, karma, the avatāras, the fate of the nondevotee — is secretly my own unasked question right now?
    • What in my life functions as the 'clothing' I am not yet willing to drop in order to become a serious student of ātma-vidyā?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Pick the one question about Kṛṣṇa, death, or purpose you would never post on social media, and ask it of one trusted devotee or teacher this week.
    • Notice how much of your identity is the 'clothing' of grades, follower counts, and friend-group status, and for one day act as if none of it were your shelter.
    • Refuse to treat spiritual class as another lecture to consume; come with one Nimi-style question written down and listen for its answer.
    householder
    • Bring your most pressing family or money question into your morning sādhana as Nimi brought his to the Yogendras, instead of separating 'spiritual life' from household decisions.
    • Identify one 'mine' in the home — a role, a possession, a control — that you hold too tightly, and loosen your grip on it today as a small offering toward vairāgya.
    • Speak to your children or spouse today about one verse or principle you are actually struggling with, not one you have mastered, modeling the seriousness of a real student.
    senior
    • Write down, in your own words, the nine questions Nimi asked, and answer them honestly for yourself as a legacy document for your family or saṅga.
    • Mentor one younger devotee this month by sitting as a Yogendra would — speaking only from śāstra and your own sādhana, not from opinion or nostalgia.
    • Begin loosening one long-held attachment — a role, a grievance, a possession — as a deliberate preparation for the final passage, and tell one person you are doing so.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Romanticizing the naked wandering of the Yogendras and confusing outward renunciation with the inward artha-śaṁsitva — the eagerness to declare the Absolute Truth.
    • Treating the list of nine names as devotional trivia to memorize, rather than as the doorway into the nine answers that follow in the next chapters.
    • Approaching the Bhāgavatam as self-improvement material instead of as a king's desperate inquiry being answered by liberated sages on behalf of all of us.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Nimi, a king, stops nine wandering naked sages and asks them direct questions about bhakti — what does it cost you, in your station of life, to ask your real questions out loud?
    • The Yogendras are described as artha-śaṁsinaḥ, eager to declare the Absolute Truth. Where in your circle is such declaration welcomed, and where is it actively unwelcome — and what does that reveal?
    • Is the Yogendras' nakedness a literal model, a symbol, or a warning against literalizing it? Disagree openly with each other before reaching for consensus.
    Role Play

    One student plays King Nimi: a busy person of responsibility with one burning, unresolved question about Kṛṣṇa, māyā, or death. Another student plays a Yogendra — not omniscient, but a serious devotee who has stopped chasing viṣaya and is willing to speak plainly. The 'king' must ask their real question; the 'Yogendra' must answer only from śāstra and lived sādhana, not from opinion. The rest of the group watches for where the 'king' softens the question and where the 'Yogendra' hides behind jargon.

    Objections & Responses
    • Why should I care about a king meeting nine naked ascetics thousands of years ago? This has nothing to do with my life.
      Nimi's nine questions — what is the highest good, how do I get free of māyā, what happens to one who turns from the Lord — are exactly the questions you ask yourself at 3 a.m. The Bhāgavatam is preserving the answers because they are still your answers; the setting is ancient, the inquiry is yours today.
    • Naked wandering sages sound like extremism. Surely a modern householder is exempt from this ideal.
      The verse honors the Yogendras' āśrama, not imposes it. Prabhupāda is careful: varṇāśrama means each person learns from the paramahaṁsa within their own station. The householder is not asked to drop clothing; they are asked to drop the inner clinging that the Yogendras dropped outwardly, and to receive ātma-vidyā with the same seriousness.

    These sages wandered the earth seeing the entire universe, with all its gross and subtle objects, as a manifestation of the Supreme Lord and as nondifferent from the self.
    Purport

    According to Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī, it is clearly demonstrated in this and the following verse that the nine saintly sons of Ṛṣabhadeva known as the nava-yogendras were situated in the highest stage of spiritual perfection, called pāramahaṁsya-caritam, or “having fully developed the character of paramahaṁsas. ” In other words, they were pure devotees of the Lord. According to Śrīdhara Svāmī and Jīva Gosvāmī, the words ātmano ’vyatirekeṇa indicate that the nine sages saw the universe as being nondifferent from themselves as well as nondifferent from the Supreme Soul, Lord Kṛṣṇa. Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura has additionally commented, ātmanaḥ paramātmanaḥ sakāśād avyatirekeṇa, viśvasya tac-chakti-mayatvād iti bhāvaḥ: “ Ātmanaḥ indicates the Supersoul. This universe is not different from the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Paramātmā, since the entire universe is composed of His energy.”

    Although it is stated here that the cosmic manifestation is nondifferent from both the living entity and the Supreme Personality of Godhead, one should not think that either the living entity or the Supreme Lord is material. A Vedic aphorism states, asaṅgo hy ayaṁ puruṣaḥ: “The living entity and the Supreme Personality of Godhead have nothing to do with the material world.” Furthermore, Bhagavad-gītā says that the entire universe, consisting of eight gross and subtle elements, constitutes the bhinnā prakṛti, or aparā prakṛti — the separated, inferior energy — of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Lord Kṛṣṇa clearly states in Bhagavad-gītā that He has eternally established His own abode in the kingdom of God, where life is eternal, full of bliss and knowledge, and that the living entity, being part and parcel of God, is also eternal ( mamaivāṁśo jīva-loke jīva-bhūtaḥ sanātanaḥ ). Furthermore, once having gone to that eternal abode of the Lord the living entity never returns to this temporary manifestation ( yaṁ prāpya na nivartante tad dhāma paramaṁ mama ).

    One may therefore ask why the living entity and the Supreme Lord are stated to be nondifferent from the material universe. The question is very nicely answered by Śrīla Nārada Muni in the First Canto of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (1.5.20) . Idaṁ hi viśvaṁ bhagavān ivetaro yato jagat-sthāna-nirodha-sambhavāḥ: “The Supreme Lord Personality of Godhead is Himself this cosmos, and still He is aloof from it. From Him only has this cosmic manifestation emanated, in Him it rests, and unto Him it enters after annihilation.” Commenting on Nārada’s statement, Śrīla Prabhupāda has very nicely explained this delicate philosophical point: “For a pure devotee, the conception of Mukunda, Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, is both personal and impersonal. The impersonal cosmic situation is also Mukunda because it is the emanation of the energy of Mukunda. For example, a tree is a complete unit, whereas the leaves and branches of the tree are emanated parts and parcels of the tree. The leaves and branches of the tree are also the tree, but the tree itself is neither the leaves nor the branches. The Vedic version that the whole cosmic creation is nothing but Brahman means that since everything is emanating from the Supreme Brahman, nothing is apart from Him. Similarly, the part-and-parcel hands and legs are called the body, but the body as the whole unit is neither the hands nor the legs. The Lord is the transcendental form of eternity, cognition and beauty. And thus the creation of the energy of the Lord appears to be partially eternal, full of knowledge and beautiful also.…

    “According to the Vedic version, the Lord is naturally fully powerful, and thus His supreme energies are always perfect and identical with Him. Both the spiritual and the material skies and their paraphernalia are emanations of the internal and external energies of the Lord. External energy is comparatively inferior, whereas the internal potency is superior. The superior energy is living force, and therefore she is completely identical [with the Lord], but the external energy, being inert, is partially identical. But both the energies are neither equal to nor greater than the Lord, who is the generator of all energies; such energies are always under His control, exactly as electrical energy, however powerful it may be, is always under the control of the engineer.

    “The human being and all other living beings are products of His internal energies. Thus the living being is also identical with the Lord. But he is never equal or superior to the Personality of Godhead.”

    Śrīla Prabhupāda has clearly explained here that both the cosmic manifestation and the living entities are emanations from the Supreme Lord, as confirmed both in Vedānta-sutra and in the opening statement of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. Janmādy asya yataḥ: “The Absolute Truth is that from which everything emanates.” Similarly, the Īśopaniṣad states:

    om pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idaṁ pūrṇāt pūrṇam udacyate pūrṇasya pūrṇam ādāya pūrṇam evāvaśiṣyate

    The Supreme Lord, the Absolute Truth, is pūrṇa, or complete in Himself. And since this cosmic world is a manifestation of His potency, it also appears to be pūrṇa. In other words, because this material world is an emanation from the Supreme Lord, it is nondifferent from Him, exactly as the sun’s rays are nondifferent from the sun globe, which is the source of their emanation. Similarly the living beings, who are expansions of the superior, or conscious, energy of the Supreme Lord, are also nondifferent from Kṛṣṇa, although this nondifference is qualitative and not quantitative. The gold found in golden ornaments such as rings and bracelets is qualitatively identical with the gold in a mine, but the gold in the mine is quantitatively far superior to the tiny quantity of gold in a bracelet or ring. Similarly, although we are qualitatively one with God, being spiritual emanations of His unlimited potency, we are quantitatively infinitesimal and eternally subordinate to His supreme power. Therefore the Lord is called vibhu, or infinitely potent, and we are aṇu, or infinitesimal and dependent. This is further confirmed in the Vedic literature by the statement nityo nityānāṁ cetanaś cetanānām/ eko bahūnāṁ yo vidadhāti kāmān ( Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.13). There are innumerable eternal living entities who are eternally and totally dependent upon the supreme singular living entity, the Supreme Lord. That dependence is not an illusion created by material existence, as stated by the impersonalist philosophers, but is an eternal relationship in which the Lord is eternally superior and we are eternally inferior. The Lord is eternally independent, and we are eternally dependent. The Lord is eternally absolute in Himself, and we are eternally relative to His supreme personality.

    Although the Lord is infinitely greater than any other living being, or than all of them combined, every living being is qualitatively nondifferent from the Lord, because all living beings are parts and parcels emanating from Him ( mamaivāṁśo jīva-loke jīva-bhūtaḥ sanātanaḥ ). Therefore, in one sense, the living entity is also not different from the material cosmic manifestation, which is an inferior sister energy of the Lord. Both the living entity and the material nature are prakṛti, or feminine, dependent expansions of the supreme puruṣa. The difference is that the living entity is the superior energy of the Lord, because the living entity is conscious and eternal like the Lord, whereas material energy is the inferior energy of the Lord, lacking consciousness and eternal form.

    Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura has emphasized in this regard that the absolute substance is one and is called Paramātmā, or the Supersoul. When one has achieved but a partial vision of the Paramātmā, one’s understanding of life is called ātma-darśana, or self-realization. And when even this partial understanding is lacking, one’s existential condition is called anātma-darśana, or ignorance of the self. In the state of partial realization of the Supersoul, without recognition of the Paramātmā’s distinction from the individual soul, the living entity tends to become puffed up by his spiritual achievement, be carried away by mental concoction, and consider himself equal in all respects with God. On the other hand, the living entity situated in anātma-darśana, or material ignorance, feels that he is completely different from the Supreme Lord; and since everyone in this material world is interested in himself, the living entity forgets about God, thinking that God is completely different from him and that there is therefore no substantial relationship between him and God. In this way the impersonal transcendentalists emphasize only the oneness between God and the living entity, whereas the ordinary materialists overemphasize the difference between God and the living entity. But Caitanya Mahāprabhu has clearly revealed that the Ultimate Truth is simultaneous oneness and difference ( acintya-bhedābheda-tattva ). Actually we are eternally different from God. Because the living entity and God are eternally separate individual entities, there exists the possibility of an eternal relationship. And because every living entity is qualitatively one with the Supreme Lord, that relationship constitutes the essence of the ultimate reality for every living being. As stated in the Caitanya-caritāmṛta ( Madhya 20.108), jīvera ‘svarūpa’ haya — kṛṣṇera ‘nitya-dāsa.’ The ultimate essential identity of every living entity is his relationship with the Supreme Lord as a servitor of the Lord.

    If one can understand that he is an eternal servant of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, one can correctly understand that both the living entity and the material universe are identical with Kṛṣṇa, being emanations from Him, and that they are therefore nondifferent from each other. Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī has stated, “The material world is a manifestation of simultaneous difference and nondifference, and it is a form of the Supreme Lord. Thus the temporary, perishable and ever-changing material world is different from Vaikuṇṭha, the eternal world.”

    It should be noted that in this verse the word sad-asad-ātmakam, or “made up of gross and subtle objects,” does not refer to material and spiritual objects. This universe is stated to be composed of sat and asat, gross and subtle material objects. According to Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī, “The very subtle state within the manifest world is known as ‘the unmanifest,’ and the realm beyond the manifest world is called ‘transcendental.’ Within the coverings surrounding the manifest, in the region of the time factor, is the phase of material existence experienced by the controlling deities; in this phase exist the two functions: cause ( asat ) and effect ( sat ). In the universe, which is a third tattva, or reality (apart from and containing both sat and asat ), and which is a form of the Supreme Lord, it is impossible to produce any contradiction to the nondual Absolute Truth.” In other words, although ignorant, materialistic scientists may zealously carry out research to find a material principle that can negate or render unnecessary the existence of God, Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī clearly states that since the universe is an emanation from the Lord and therefore spiritually identical with Him, there cannot possibly exist anywhere within the universe a material law, principle or phenomenon that in any way contradicts the supremacy of the Personality of Godhead. In fact, the entire universe, along with the spiritual sky, exists as eternal testimony to the unlimited glory of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Kṛṣṇa. With this understanding, the nine Yogendras were traveling about the earth in transcendental bliss.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    These sages wandered the earth while seeing the entire universe, with all its gross and subtle objects, as a manifestation of the Supreme Lord and as nondifferent from Paramātmā. Ātmanaḥ means Paramātmā. They saw the universe as identical with Paramātmā since it is his śakti.

    Personal Guidance
    See the world as Kṛṣṇa's energy — nondifferent from Him yet not Him — and walk the earth as His eternal servant in acintya-bhedābheda.
    Practical Applications
    • Today, when you handle any object — phone, food, money — pause and recognize it as Kṛṣṇa's energy, not raw matter to exploit.
    • Refuse two impersonal slips this week: catching yourself say 'the universe' or 'consciousness' when you mean Kṛṣṇa, and correct it inwardly.
    • Before sleep, recall jīvera svarūpa haya kṛṣṇera nitya-dāsa — name yourself as His eternal servant, not as the controller of your day.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do I still treat the material world as if it were separate from Kṛṣṇa — something to manage on my own terms rather than His energy?
    • Do I drift into oneness-thinking that flatters me as equal to God, or into difference-thinking that severs me from Him — and which is more habitual?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When a class, an app, or a friend group feels meaningless, remember it is Kṛṣṇa's energy you are moving through — not a flat material backdrop to your ambition.
    • Refuse the campus impersonalism that says 'we're all just consciousness, man' — keep Kṛṣṇa's personal name on your tongue, even quietly.
    • Before posting, scrolling, or comparing yourself online, name yourself as His aṇu servant — not the vibhu protagonist of your feed.
    householder
    • Treat the home — spouse, children, bills, kitchen — as Kṛṣṇa's energy entrusted to you, not as private property you alone are managing.
    • When work or money pressure tempts you to see colleagues and clients as mere instruments, recover the vision that each is a soul, eternally His.
    • Establish one daily family moment — a verse, a meal offered, a kīrtana — where the household explicitly remembers it is His, not yours.
    senior
    • As you loosen grip on assets, roles, and reputation, practice seeing each as His energy returning to its source — not as 'mine' being lost.
    • When mentoring children or grandchildren, transmit the personalist vision: He is Kṛṣṇa, not 'the universe' — give them a Name to call on.
    • Facing the body's decline, anchor in nityo nityānāṁ — you are eternal, dependent, His servant — and let that, not nostalgia, frame your remaining years.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading ātmano 'vyatirekeṇa as license for 'I am God' monism, forgetting the eternal vibhu–aṇu distinction the paramahaṁsas held.
    • Using 'everything is Kṛṣṇa's energy' to justify sense indulgence — eating, spending, scrolling — under a thin spiritual veneer.
    • Imagining the nava-yogendras' vision is a meditative technique to practice, rather than the fruit of paramahaṁsya-caritam built on sādhana and surrender.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Where do you actually live — in oneness-overreach, in difference-forgetfulness of Kṛṣṇa, or somewhere honest in between? Name the evidence.
    • If the universe is nondifferent from Kṛṣṇa, why does Caitanya Mahāprabhu still call this world temporary and Vaikuṇṭha eternal? Argue both sides.
    • Share a moment this week when you treated a person or object as inert matter rather than as Kṛṣṇa's energy. What changed when you reframed it?
    Role Play

    One student plays a friend who says, 'I read some Vedānta — everything is one, you and I and that tree are all God, so why bother with this Kṛṣṇa-devotion business?' The other student, drawing on acintya-bhedābheda and the vibhu–aṇu distinction, must respond as a fellow practitioner — not lecturing, but showing why the oneness this verse describes still demands surrender to Kṛṣṇa personally.

    Objections & Responses
    • This is just pantheism dressed in Sanskrit — if the universe is nondifferent from God, you've collapsed Creator into creation.
      Acintya-bhedābheda holds both at once: the universe emanates from Kṛṣṇa and is therefore nondifferent in source, yet He remains the puruṣa, eternally aloof, infinitely greater. The gold ornament and the gold mine share substance, not magnitude. Pantheism erases the difference; this verse preserves it.
    • Seeing everything as the Lord sounds nice but is useless in actual life — I still have to pay rent, treat illness, deal with rude people.
      Precisely — the nava-yogendras were not floating; they were walking the earth (vyacaran mahīm). The vision does not exempt you from action, it changes who you are acting toward. The rude person is still rude, but no longer merely an obstacle — they are a soul, dependent on the same Kṛṣṇa you are.

    The nine Yogendras are liberated souls who travel freely to the planets of the demigods, the perfected mystics, the Sādhyas, the heavenly musicians, the Yakṣas, the human beings, and the minor demigods such as the Kinnaras and the serpents.     Translation
    The nine Yogendras are liberated souls who travel unchecked to the planets of the devatās, the perfected mystics, the Sādhyas, the heavenly musicians, the Yakṣas, the human beings, and the Kinnaras and the serpents. As they wish, they can travel as well to the worlds of the sages, the Cāraṇas, the ghostly followers of Lord Śiva, the Vidyādharas, the brāhmaṇas and the cows.
    Related lectures

      His Holiness Vedavyasa Priya Swami· English

      His Holiness Vedavyasa Priya Swami· 2008-09-20· English
    Personal Guidance
    Liberation in bhakti is not confinement but unimpeded freedom — the Yogendras roam every world at will because nothing material can check a surrendered soul.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where you feel 'stuck' — by job, body, circumstance — and recognize that the cage is identification with matter, not the soul itself.
    • Refuse the modern belief that freedom means more options; instead, take one act of surrender to Kṛṣṇa and feel the freedom that follows.
    • Speak to someone you envy for their mobility or status, and silently remember that the liberated soul moves where even they cannot.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which 'planets' of pleasure, recognition, or security have I been straining to reach, while ignoring the freedom offered through bhakti?
    • What would my day look like if I lived as someone whose movement no mundane force can check — not in body, but in consciousness?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When peers measure freedom by where they can travel, who they can date, what they can post — notice that the verse describes a freedom none of that can buy.
    • Pick the rule in your sādhana you most resent (early rising, no intoxication, restraint on phone) and keep it strictly for one week as an experiment in real freedom.
    • Refuse the FOMO economy of social media: every scroll is an attempt to visit 'planets' you were never meant to chase.
    householder
    • When the mortgage, the school run, and the office make you feel caged, remember the cage is identification — do your duty with the inner freedom of one who is not the doer.
    • Decide one family expenditure this month not by 'what will the neighbors think' but by 'what would a soul unconstrained by material opinion choose?'
    • Speak to your spouse and children today as eternal souls passing through your household, not as fixtures whose behavior must conform to your expectations.
    senior
    • As the body's mobility narrows, deliberately widen the soul's mobility — japa, hearing, and remembrance go where the legs no longer can.
    • Loosen your grip on the house, the bank account, the family role; the Yogendras hold nothing and are welcome everywhere.
    • Mentor a younger devotee by transmitting not your achievements but the taste of an unconstrained inner life, which is the only inheritance that travels with the soul.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Romanticizing the Yogendras' travel as a yogic siddhi to acquire, rather than the natural byproduct of pure devotion.
    • Mistaking liberation for escapism — wanting to flee responsibilities instead of being free *within* one's duties.
    • Treating 'free movement' as license for whim, when the verse describes movement governed entirely by Kṛṣṇa's pleasure (kāmam, in the highest sense).
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a time you felt most 'unfree' — was the obstacle outside you, or inside? What would the verse say to that moment?
    • The verse lists realms most of us will never see. Why does Vyāsa bother describing them, and what does it do to our scale of values?
    • If a liberated soul can already roam every world, what is left for him to want? Discuss what motivates the muktas to keep acting at all.
    Role Play

    A college student tells her devotee friend she is leaving sādhana because it feels restrictive — early mornings, dietary rules, no parties. The friend must use this verse to show her that the rules are not the cage; her current life is. Play both roles for five minutes, then switch.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like mythology — demigods, Yakṣas, Kinnaras. Why should a modern student take seriously a verse about beings we cannot verify?
      Set aside the cosmology for a moment and notice the structural claim: there exist states of consciousness that no material force can constrain. That claim is testable in your own life — try one week of disciplined sādhana and see whether your inner mobility expands or contracts. The cosmology is the map; bhakti is the territory.
    • If the Yogendras are already liberated and can go anywhere, isn't this just spiritual tourism dressed up as mokṣa?
      Their movement is not for sense-gratification but for the welfare of others — they appear in Janaka's court precisely to teach. Liberation in the Gauḍīya line is never a private vacation; it is freedom *for* service. The mukta moves where Kṛṣṇa's mission calls him, which is why even the brāhmaṇa and cow communities are listed alongside the celestial realms.

    Once in Ajanābha [the former name of the earth], they came upon the sacrificial performance of the great soul Mahārāja Nimi, which was being carried out under the direction of elevated sages.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Once in Ajanābha (Bhārata-varṣa), they came upon the sacrificial performance of the great soul Mahārāja Nimi, which was being carried out under the direction of sages.
    Personal Guidance
    Great souls arrive 'by yadṛcchā' where genuine sacrifice is going on — show up to real sādhana, and the saintly will find you there.
    Practical Applications
    • Pick one ongoing sacrifice in your life — japa, study, service — and keep it lit today, even when no one is watching.
    • Refuse the calculation that sādhus only appear in famous places; receive every association that comes 'unsought' today as a real visit.
    • Speak to one person engaged in honest spiritual effort today and offer concrete help to keep their sacrifice running.
    Reflection Questions
    • What sacrifice in my life is genuine enough that a Nava-yogī could walk into it tomorrow without me having to rearrange anything?
    • Where am I waiting for the 'right' saint or setting before I start, instead of starting where I stand so that the right ones can arrive?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Keep one small daily practice — a fixed round of japa, a Gītā śloka, a quiet morning — running through exam week, not just on retreat weekends.
    • Stop waiting for the 'right' satsaṅga group on campus; start a simple weekly reading with two friends and let the right people walk in.
    • When an unexpected encounter with a serious devotee comes through a hostel, a class, or social media, treat it as a real visit, not a coincidence to scroll past.
    householder
    • Establish one non-negotiable family sacrifice this week — a short evening kīrtana, a shared verse at dinner — and protect it from work and errands.
    • Open your home to one practitioner this month, even briefly, so that your household becomes the kind of place where great souls could plausibly arrive.
    • When a saintly visitor or teacher comes 'by chance' through travel, family, or work, rearrange the calendar to receive them rather than treating it as an interruption.
    senior
    • Use this season to keep a steady, visible sādhana in the home so that children and grandchildren see a sacrifice quietly being maintained.
    • Mentor at least one younger practitioner in the discipline of daily yajña, transmitting not theory but the habit of keeping the fire lit.
    • Loosen attachment to choosing who your associates will be in your final years; trust that yadṛcchayā will bring the right souls if your sādhana is real.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating 'yadṛcchayā' as random luck and so making no effort to maintain a steady sacrifice in the first place.
    • Romanticizing the visit of great souls while neglecting the unglamorous daily yajña that makes such a visit possible.
    • Assuming great souls only come to the famous and the qualified, and so dismissing the humble sādhana already in front of you.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a time something spiritually significant came to you 'unsought' — and honestly examine what sacrifice you were already performing that made it possible.
    • Mahārāja Nimi's satra was led by elevated sages even before the Nava-yogīs arrived — discuss the difference between seeking association and building a sacrifice worth visiting.
    • Where in our community is the 'satra' that a wandering sādhu would actually want to step into, and where is it merely a performance?
    Role Play

    One student plays a sincere practitioner running a small, unglamorous weekly kīrtana in their home; another plays a visitor who arrived only because a friend's car broke down nearby. Enact the first ten minutes after the visitor steps in — how does the host receive an 'unsought' guest as a real arrival, and how does the visitor recognize the sacrifice they've stumbled into?

    Objections & Responses
    • This verse is just narrative scene-setting — a king's sacrifice, some sages dropping by. What guidance is actually here?
      The Gauḍīya reading does not split 'narrative' from 'instruction.' That great souls came yadṛcchayā precisely where a sacrifice was being maintained by elevated sages is the teaching: keep the yajña burning, and the meeting Kṛṣṇa wants for you will arrange itself.
    • If everything happens yadṛcchayā, why bother with the discipline of a daily sādhana at all?
      Yadṛcchayā describes the arrival of the sādhus, not the existence of the sacrifice. Nimi and the ṛṣis had already organized and were sustaining the satra; the 'unsought' grace landed on a fire that was already lit by their effort.

    My dear King, seeing those pure devotees of the Lord, who rival the sun in brilliance, everyone present — the performer of the sacrifice, the brāhmaṇas and even the sacrificial fires — stood in respect.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    My dear King, seeing those pure devotees of the Lord, who rival the sun in brilliance, everyone present—the performer of the sacrifice, the brāhmaṇas and even the sacrificial fires—stood in respect.
    Personal Guidance
    When pure devotees of Kṛṣṇa arrive, even the priests, the patron, and the sacrificial fires rise — devotee-darśana outranks every ritual in progress.
    Practical Applications
    • Pause whatever 'important' task you are doing today the moment a sincere devotee enters the room, and offer your full attention as a small standing-up of the heart.
    • Identify one mahā-bhāgavata-class soul in your life (a guru, a senior Vaiṣṇava) and physically rise, fold your hands, or bow when you next meet them, however ordinary the setting.
    • Refuse to rank your daily sādhana — japa, study, work — above the rare chance to serve or hear from an advanced devotee.
    Reflection Questions
    • Whose presence in my life already shines like the sun, and how am I still seated — distracted, unmoved — when they speak?
    • What 'sacrifice' of mine (career, routine, even worship) have I been protecting so fiercely that I would not interrupt it for a pure devotee?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When a senior devotee or genuinely God-conscious elder visits your college or family, put the phone face-down and stand up — let your body lead where your distracted mind cannot.
    • Notice the difference between the friends you 'rise' for (popular, useful) and the quiet devotee classmate you overlook, and reverse that ranking for one week.
    • Refuse to treat your exams or career-prep as so urgent that you skip the rare evening when an advanced Vaiṣṇava is speaking nearby.
    householder
    • When a senior Vaiṣṇava visits your home, interrupt the work call, the cooking, even the children's routine, and let your whole family see you rise first.
    • Audit the calendar: are quarterly reviews and school meetings non-negotiable while devotee-saṅga is 'if there's time'? Re-rank one slot this month.
    • Teach your children by example — explain why you stood up when that particular uncle or sannyāsī walked in, so they learn whom to honor and why.
    senior
    • Use the remaining years to actively seek out and physically attend on mahā-bhāgavatas; do not let stiffness of body or pride of seniority keep you seated.
    • Loosen attachment to your own decades of 'sacrifice' — service, donations, positions — by deferring publicly to a more advanced devotee in your circle.
    • Mentor younger devotees specifically in the art of recognizing and rising for Vaiṣṇavas, so this culture does not die with your generation.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reducing the verse to mere etiquette — standing up mechanically — while inwardly continuing to rank yourself above the devotee.
    • Imagining mahā-bhāgavatas as figures only from the past, so you never have to actually recognize and honor one walking among you now.
    • Treating your own sādhana or seva as so sacred that even a senior Vaiṣṇava's arrival becomes an 'interruption' rather than the higher event.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a moment you failed to recognize an advanced devotee in front of you — what were you protecting in yourself by staying seated?
    • If even the sacrificial fires stood up, what does that say about the relative weight of ritual versus devotee-association in our own practice?
    • How do we distinguish genuine reverence for a mahā-bhāgavata from social performance or sectarian hero-worship?
    Role Play

    A busy temple president is mid-meeting about a fundraising deadline when an elderly, unannounced Vaiṣṇava — known to be deeply advanced but socially awkward — walks in. One student plays the president, another the visiting devotee, a third a junior devotee watching. Enact the next two minutes: who rises, who keeps typing, what is said, and what the room learns.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like a caste-style demand to bow to 'holy men' — isn't that exactly the kind of hierarchy modern people should resist?
      The verse is not about social rank but about recognizing the rare soul in whom Kṛṣṇa is fully manifest; standing up is the body finally agreeing with what the heart already knows. We rise not because they demand it but because their presence reorients us toward Kṛṣṇa, the way a room turns toward sunrise.
    • If even the brāhmaṇas and fires stand, the verse seems to glorify devotees over the Vedic process itself — isn't that contradictory?
      Not contradictory but climactic: the whole purpose of yajña is to please Kṛṣṇa, and a mahā-bhāgavata is His direct representative. The fires are not being demoted; they are showing us, in dramatic form, that the living embodiment of bhakti is the goal toward which all ritual was always pointing.

    King Videha [Nimi] understood that the nine sages were exalted devotees of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Therefore, overjoyed at their auspicious arrival, he offered them suitable sitting places and worshiped them in a proper way, just as one would worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead.
    Purport

    The word yathārhataḥ is significant here. According to Viśvanātha Cakravartī the word yathārhataḥ means yathocitam, or “according to the proper etiquette.” It is clearly mentioned here that the nava-yogendras are nārāyaṇa-parāyaṇa, exalted devotees of the Supreme Lord, Nārāyaṇa, or Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, the word yathārhataḥ indicates that the King worshiped the nine sages according to the standard Vaiṣṇava etiquette. The etiquette for worshiping exalted Vaiṣṇavas is expressed by Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura with the words sākṣād-dharitvena samasta-śāstraiḥ: an exalted Vaiṣṇava, being totally surrendered to the will of the Supreme Lord, is taken to be a transparent medium for the Lord’s will. In the Caitanya-caritāmṛta it is stated that even by a moment’s association with the pure devotees of the Lord one can achieve all perfection in life. Therefore, as indicated by the word prītaḥ, King Nimi was overjoyed by the auspicious arrival of the sages, and therefore he worshiped them just as one would worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

    Although impersonalist philosophers claim that every living entity is equal to God, they callously step over the heads of their so-called spiritual masters and freely speculate on the nature of the Absolute, giving their own whimsical opinions in defiance of the impersonal whims of their so-called gurus. In other words, although Māyāvādī impersonalists claim that everyone is God, they ultimately show an offensive mentality toward the Supreme Personality of Godhead in rejecting the reality of His eternal form and pastimes. Thus, they unwittingly belittle the eternal position of all living beings by denying their eternal personality and activities in the kingdom of God. The impersonalists, through their mental concoctions, try to minimize the position of the Supreme Personality of Godhead and the living entities who are part of Him, reducing them theoretically to a formless, nameless light, which by their concoction they claim to be the Absolute God. The Vaiṣṇavas, however, welcome the Supreme Personality of Godhead and easily understand that the unlimited Supreme Personality has nothing to do with the conditioned, limited, mundane personalities we find in the material world. The impersonalists arrogantly assume that there could not be any transcendental or unlimited personality beyond our present experience. But the Vaiṣṇavas intelligently understand that there are many wonderful things far beyond our limited experience. Therefore they accept the words of Kṛṣṇa, who states in Bhagavad-gītā (15.19) :

    yo mām evam asammūḍho jānāti puruṣottamam sa sarva-vid bhajati māṁ sarva-bhāvena bhārata

    “Whoever knows Me as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, without doubting, is the knower of everything, and he therefore engages himself in full devotional service, O son of Bharata.” In this connection Śrīla Prabhupāda states, “There are many philosophical speculations about the constitutional position of the living entities and the Supreme Absolute Truth. Now in this verse the Supreme Personality of Godhead clearly explains that anyone who knows Lord Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Person is actually the knower of everything. The imperfect knower goes on simply speculating about the Absolute Truth, but the perfect knower, without wasting his valuable time, engages directly in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, the devotional service of the Supreme Lord.… It is not that one should simply speculate academically. One should submissively hear from Bhagavad-gītā that these living entities are always subordinate to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Anyone who is able to understand this, according to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, knows the purpose of the Vedas; no one else knows the purpose of the Vedas. ” Therefore, exalted devotees such as the nine Yogendras always accept the supremacy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as expressed here by the word nārāyaṇa-parāyaṇān.

    King Nimi was a Vaiṣṇava, and therefore he worshiped the great sages with the same respect with which he would worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as shown by the word yathārhataḥ. Although impersonalists falsely claim that every living entity is equal to God, they cannot properly respect any living being, because of their original offense at the lotus feet of the Supreme Personality. Their so-called worship, even of their own gurus, is ultimately self-serving and opportunistic. When an impersonalist imagines that he has become God, he has no further need for his so-called guru. The Vaiṣṇava, however, because he accepts the supremacy of the eternal Personality of Godhead, is ready and willing to offer eternal respect to all living beings, especially to those most fortunate living beings who have achieved shelter at the lotus feet of the Lord. A Vaiṣṇava’s worship of the Lord’s representative is not self-serving or opportunistic, but is an expression of eternal love for the Lord and His representatives, as indicated here by the word prītaḥ. Therefore it is clear from this verse that not only the nine exalted sons of Ṛṣabhadeva but also King Nimi himself were all great devotees of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, in defiance of the artificial and limited concept of impersonalism.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda

    Translation
    King Nimi understood that the nine sages were exalted devotees of Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, overjoyed at their auspicious arrival, he offered them suitable sitting places and worshiped them in the proper way. Yathārhataḥ means “properly.”
    Related lectures
    • BKG SB 11-02-26 - 2012-05-01 New Talavan
      His Holiness Bir Krishna Goswami· 2012-05-01· English
    Personal Guidance
    Recognize a pure devotee as a transparent medium of Kṛṣṇa and honor them with the same reverence due to the Lord Himself.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify one devotee in your life who is nārāyaṇa-parāyaṇa and offer them a concrete act of service or respect today — a meal, a seat, attentive hearing.
    • Drop the impersonalist habit of equalizing everyone; train your eyes to recognize and honor the specific living beings who have taken shelter of Kṛṣṇa.
    • Before any spiritual conversation today, mentally bow to the devotee speaking and receive their words as a transparent medium for the Lord's will.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do I withhold proper Vaiṣṇava etiquette from devotees because I privately judge myself their equal or superior?
    • What would change in my day if I genuinely treated even one devotee's arrival as the auspicious arrival King Nimi felt?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When an older devotee or sincere senior visits your hostel or home, put down the phone, stand up, offer a seat, and actually listen — practice yathārhataḥ in a setting your friends will notice.
    • Audit your social media feeds: unfollow one impersonalist 'we are all one' influencer and replace them with a source rooted in Kṛṣṇa-bhakti.
    • In your friend group, refuse the lazy egalitarianism that treats every opinion as equal — quietly give more weight to the friend who is actually trying to serve Kṛṣṇa.
    householder
    • Make your home a place where visiting devotees are received with a clean seat, prasāda, and undivided attention — schedule it like you would an important client.
    • Teach your children by example to bow and offer respect to senior Vaiṣṇavas, naming for them why this person is worthy of honor.
    • Budget time and money this month specifically for hosting or supporting a nārāyaṇa-parāyaṇa devotee, rather than only on family-internal comforts.
    senior
    • Use your remaining years to seek out and sit with devotees more advanced than you, rather than settling into the role of the one always being honored.
    • Mentor a younger devotee in the concrete etiquette of receiving Vaiṣṇavas — āsana, words, tone — so the standard outlives you.
    • Loosen attachment to being treated as the senior in the room; instead, model how a Vaiṣṇava honors others as transparent mediums of Kṛṣṇa.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Confusing Vaiṣṇava reverence with sentimental flattery — bowing externally while withholding real submission and service.
    • Slipping into the impersonalist reflex that 'everyone is equally God,' which flattens the special position of those surrendered to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Reserving such honor only for famous or robed devotees while ignoring the unassuming nārāyaṇa-parāyaṇa already in your home or saṅga.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a time you failed to recognize a devotee in front of you — what blinded you, and what would yathārhataḥ have looked like in that moment?
    • Where is the line between worshiping a Vaiṣṇava as a transparent medium of Kṛṣṇa and the offense of worshiping a person as God? Disagree honestly with your partner.
    • If 'a moment's association with a pure devotee' can grant all perfection, why does our actual time with devotees so often feel ordinary — what are we doing wrong?
    Role Play

    An unannounced senior devotee arrives at your home during a busy workday — children are noisy, dinner is half-cooked, and you have a deadline in an hour. Show how you would receive, seat, and honor them yathārhataḥ, and narrate aloud what you are choosing to set aside and why.

    Objections & Responses
    • Treating one human as a 'transparent medium' of God is exactly the kind of guru-worship that leads to cults and abuse — safer to keep everyone equal.
      The verse does not authorize blind worship of anyone in saffron; it specifies nārāyaṇa-parāyaṇān — those visibly surrendered to Kṛṣṇa and bound by śāstra. Vaiṣṇava etiquette honors the Lord's will operating through such a person, not their personality, and śāstra itself is the check against the abuses you rightly fear.
    • Why elaborate reception, seating, and worship? Surely Kṛṣṇa cares about inner attitude, not whether I offered the right cushion.
      Inner attitude expresses itself through the body, or it is not yet real. King Nimi was prītaḥ — overjoyed — and that joy naturally took form as proper etiquette. Skipping the outward forms usually means the inward bhāva has not yet matured; the forms are how we train it.

    Overwhelmed by transcendental joy, the King humbly bowed his head and then proceeded to question the nine sages. These nine great souls glowed with their own effulgence and thus appeared equal to the four Kumāras, the sons of Lord Brahmā.
    Purport

    Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī has pointed out that the word sva-rucā indicates that the nava-yogendras glowed from their own spiritual effulgence and not due to their ornaments or any other cause. The Supreme Soul, Lord Kṛṣṇa, is the original source of all light. His brilliantly glowing body is the source of the all-pervading brahmajyoti, the immeasurable spiritual light that is the resting place of innumerable universes ( yasya prabhā prabhavato jagad-aṇḍa-koṭi ). The individual soul, being part and parcel of the Lord, is also self-effulgent. In fact, everything in the kingdom of God is self-effulgent, as described in Bhagavad-gītā (15.6) :

    na tad bhāsayate sūryo na śaśāṅko na pāvakaḥ yad gatvā na nivartante tad dhāma paramaṁ mama

    It has already been described in many ways that the nava-yogendras were pure devotees of the Lord. Being completely Kṛṣṇa conscious souls, they naturally radiated the intense effulgence of the soul, as indicated here by the word sva-rucā. Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī has also pointed out that the word brahma-putropamān, meaning “equal to the sons of Brahmā,” indicates that the nava-yogendras were on the same spiritual platform as the four exalted Kumāra brothers. It has been described in the Fourth Canto that Mahārāja Pṛthu received the four Kumāras with great love and reverence, and here King Nimi is similarly receiving the nine sons of Lord Ṛṣabhadeva. Receiving exalted Vaiṣṇavas with love and reverence is standard spiritual etiquette for those who desire progress and happiness in life.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda

    Personal Guidance
    When self-effulgent devotees arrive, bow first and ask after — reverent inquiry from the humbled head is the gateway to real knowledge.
    Practical Applications
    • When you meet an advanced devotee today, physically bow your head before saying anything, and let your first words be a sincere question, not a self-introduction.
    • Notice whose 'glow' you are drawn to — entertainers, influencers, the wealthy — and redirect that same attention toward Vaiṣṇavas whose effulgence is sva-rucā, from the soul.
    • Refuse to approach scripture or a teacher casually; before your next class or reading, take one minute to settle into praśraya — the bowed posture of a learner.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I posturing as a peer or critic with devotees and teachers, when the verse asks me to stand as a humble inquirer with bowed head?
    • What would change in how I receive a sādhu's words if I actually believed, like King Nimi, that their effulgence comes from the soul and not from their credentials or charisma?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • On campus or online, notice which classmates and influencers you instinctively look up to, and ask honestly whether their 'glow' is sva-rucā or just packaging — then spend an hour this week with someone whose light is quieter and more real.
    • Before your next class, exam prep session, or conversation with a mentor, take ten seconds to mentally bow your head and frame an actual question — not a performance of one — and watch how much more you absorb.
    • Refuse the peer-group habit of mocking or 'roasting' anyone older or more serious; even silent reverence in your body language begins to rewire how knowledge reaches you.
    householder
    • When a Vaiṣṇava — a visiting devotee, a guest, even a serious practitioner among your friends — comes to your home, personally receive them at the door, bow, and let your children see you do it; reception is taught more than told.
    • Before a hard family decision about money, career, or children, identify one mature devotee you can humbly inquire from this week, and approach them parama-prītaḥ — not to validate a decision you've already made.
    • Notice when your professional authority leaks into your spiritual life — speaking to teachers as peers or vendors — and deliberately recover the bowed-head posture in those exchanges.
    senior
    • Resist the elder's temptation to be the one always teaching; this week, deliberately seek out a devotee — possibly younger in years — whose effulgence is sva-rucā, bow internally, and ask one real question.
    • As you mentor children, grandchildren, or younger seekers, model what King Nimi modeled: show them how a person of stature still bows the head before truth, so they learn humility by watching, not by lecturing.
    • Loosen attachment to your accumulated credentials and stature; let the final chapter of your life be characterized by praśraya — the bowed posture of an inquirer — rather than the upright posture of an authority.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking outward humility — folded hands, sweet words — for the inward praśraya that actually empties the cup before asking.
    • Reserving reverence only for famous or institutionally-titled devotees and missing the self-effulgent Vaiṣṇava who arrives without fanfare.
    • Asking questions to display one's own learning or to test the teacher, instead of asking parama-prītaḥ — overwhelmed by the joy of their presence.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a time you met someone whose 'light' you sensed was sva-rucā — from the soul — versus borrowed from position or personality. How did you behave differently in each case?
    • King Nimi was himself a great king, yet he bowed his head before asking. Where in your life does your status or expertise stop you from taking the posture of a learner — and is that protecting you or costing you?
    • The verse links bowing first and questioning second. Discuss: is it possible to receive real spiritual knowledge without first surrendering posture, or is the bow non-negotiable?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. One plays a busy professional who has just been introduced to a quiet, unassuming Vaiṣṇava at a program — no titles, no entourage, only sva-rucā. The other plays the Vaiṣṇava. The professional has fifteen minutes and a list of questions about life direction. Practice the opening sixty seconds: how do you greet, what does your body do, and what is your first sentence? Then swap. Debrief on what felt natural, what felt forced, and where ahaṅkāra showed up.

    Objections & Responses
    • Bowing the head to another human being is degrading — I respect people as equals, not as superiors.
      The bow in this verse is not to a body or a social superior; it is to the soul's effulgence shining through a surrendered devotee, and ultimately to Kṛṣṇa within them. King Nimi was a sovereign — he lost nothing by bowing, because he was honoring the source of all light, not abasing himself before a man. Refusing to bow protects ahaṅkāra, not dignity.
    • I can read books and watch lectures online — why do I need to physically approach and inquire from a sādhu at all?
      Information can travel through a screen, but the transmission described here — parama-prītaḥ, overwhelmed joy in the presence of self-effulgent devotees — cannot. The verse shows knowledge passing through a specific channel: bowed head, humble inquiry, living association. Bypass that channel and you may accumulate facts, but you will not receive what King Nimi received from the nava-yogendras.

    King Videha said: I think that you must be direct associates of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is famous as the enemy of the demon Madhu. Indeed, the pure devotees of Lord Viṣṇu wander throughout the universe not for their personal, selfish interest, but to purify all the conditioned souls.
    Purport

    King Nimi here welcomes the great sages by glorifying their transcendental activities. It is well known that the Supreme Personality of Godhead is transcendental to the three modes of material nature, as stated in Bhagavad-gītā (7.13) : mām ebhyaḥ param avyayam. Similarly, His pure devotees are also on the transcendental platform. One may ask how such transcendental living beings as the associates of Lord Viṣṇu could be seen within the material world. Therefore it is stated here, pāvanāya caranti hi: the associates of Lord Viṣṇu travel throughout the universe to reclaim the fallen, conditioned souls on behalf of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. A representative of the governor may be seen moving within the prison house, but that does not mean that the governor’s representative has become a conditioned prisoner. It is understood that he is within the prison to negotiate the possible release of those prisoners who have rectified their criminal propensity. Similarly, the devotees of the Supreme Personality of Godhead called parivrājakācāryas wander throughout the universe inviting everyone to surrender to Lord Kṛṣṇa and go back home, back to Godhead, for an eternal life of bliss and knowledge.

    In the Sixth Canto of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam the mercy of the associates of Lord Viṣṇu has been described in connection with the salvation of Ajāmila. Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura has pointed out that the associates of Lord Viṣṇu are as merciful as the Lord Himself. Even though the ignorant members of human society are not interested in approaching the servants of Lord Viṣṇu, the devotees of the Lord, without any false prestige, act to liberate the conditioned souls from their perpetual misfortune.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    King Nimi said: I think that you must be direct associates of the Supreme Lord, who is famous as the enemy of the demon Madhu. The pure devotees of Lord Viṣṇu wander throughout the universe to purify all the conditioned souls. Two verses describe how the King welcomed them. “Why would the associates of Viṣṇu come here?” The associates (bhūtāni) of Viṣṇu move about to purify the worlds with their mercy.
    Related lectures
    • JAS SB 11-02-28 - Why Saintly Devotees Travel - 2017-04-12 ISKCON Chowpatty
      His Holiness Jayadvaita Swami· 2017-04-12· English
    Personal Guidance
    Pure devotees of Viṣṇu wander not for themselves but to purify the fallen — receive them as Kṛṣṇa's direct associates, not ordinary men.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify one Vaiṣṇava who has tried to help you spiritually and write to thank them today, treating that contact as Kṛṣṇa's outreach to you.
    • Refuse the habit of evaluating preachers and sādhus by worldly criteria — wealth, charisma, credentials — and instead ask whether their movement is to reclaim conditioned souls.
    • When you next speak to someone about Kṛṣṇa, drop any personal angle (looking wise, gaining a friend) and speak only for their pāvana — their purification.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I quietly resisting the mercy of devotees because receiving it would expose my conditioned status as a prisoner?
    • If Viṣṇu's associates walk the world only to purify others, what does that reveal about the smallness of my own self-interested 'service'?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When an older devotee at the temple or on campus offers you time, drop the instinct to perform or impress and simply ask one honest question about your actual life.
    • Unfollow one influencer whose 'wisdom' is built on self-promotion, and in that slot subscribe to a lecture by a parivrājaka who is asking nothing of you but your hearing.
    • Notice when you describe a sādhu to your friends using social-media categories ('he's kind of famous,' 'his following is small') and retrain yourself to ask only whether he is pointing you toward Kṛṣṇa.
    householder
    • Invite a travelling devotee for prasāda in your home this month and arrange the visit around your children's presence, so they see what a Vaiṣṇava actually is rather than hearing about it.
    • When a devotee gives you spiritual advice that crosses your career or financial plans, do not file it under 'nice but impractical' — sit with it for a week before deciding.
    • Audit the people you currently call mentors: how many are working for your pāvana versus your worldly advancement, and which group are you giving more of your attention to?
    senior
    • Use the freedom of this stage to actively seek the company of parivrājakas — attend a festival, host a programme, travel to where they are — rather than waiting for them to find you.
    • Make a quiet resolution that the remaining years are for your own purification and for purifying others, not for legacy projects centred on your name.
    • When younger family members dismiss visiting devotees as 'just monks,' do not argue — share one specific verse or pastime that helped you, and let the example of your reception of those devotees teach more than your words.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking the devotee's presence in the material world as proof that he is materially conditioned, and so dismissing his instructions.
    • Welcoming devotees with King Nimi's words on the tongue while privately treating them as ordinary guests to be impressed or managed.
    • Aspiring to 'wander and purify others' before one has himself surrendered to Kṛṣṇa, turning the verse into a license for premature preaching.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a time you encountered a devotee and only later realized who they were — what did you miss in the moment, and why?
    • King Nimi recognizes the sages immediately; most of us would not. What in our own consciousness blocks that recognition, and is it removable?
    • Is it possible to be a 'representative of the governor' in the prison house of one's own family or workplace without becoming a fellow prisoner — what would that actually look like this week?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. One plays a busy professional who has just been approached at the door by a saffron-clad devotee offering a book; the other plays the devotee, whose only motive is the householder's pāvana, not a sale or a number. Run the exchange twice — once with the householder dismissive, once with him cautiously curious — and afterwards discuss what shifted in the devotee's bearing when he held strictly to 'not for personal interest.'

    Objections & Responses
    • Every religious group claims its missionaries are selfless — why should I treat wandering Vaiṣṇavas as different from any other proselytizers knocking on doors?
      The test is not the claim but the content of what is offered. A parivrājakācārya is not recruiting you to a tribe or asking for your loyalty to him; he is asking you to surrender to Kṛṣṇa and return home. If a person's whole movement is to hand you over to the Supreme Personality of Godhead and take nothing for himself, that is by definition not proselytizing in the ordinary sense — it is the governor's representative inside the prison.
    • If these devotees are already transcendental, why do they bother with us? Isn't the whole 'come purify the fallen' framing a bit condescending?
      It would be condescending if it came from a fellow prisoner pretending to be free. But the verse describes those who are actually liberated descending voluntarily, the way Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura points out the associates of Viṣṇu are as merciful as the Lord Himself. The condescension you sense is your own ahaṅkāra resisting the diagnosis — 'fallen' is not an insult, it is the accurate description of a conditioned soul, and refusing the diagnosis is what keeps the cell door shut.

    For the conditioned souls, the human body is most difficult to achieve, and it can be lost at any moment. But I think that even those who have achieved human life rarely gain the association of pure devotees, who are dear to the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha.
    Purport

    According to Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī, the word dehinām means bahavo dehā bhavanti yeṣāṁ te, “the conditioned souls, who accept innumerable material bodies.” According to some wishful thinkers a living entity in the human form of life will never be degraded to a lower form such as that of an animal or plant. But despite this wishful thinking, it is a fact that according to our activities at the present, we will be elevated or degraded by the laws of God. At the present time in human society there is no clear or precise understanding of the nature of life. Foolish scientists have invented highly sophisticated terminologies and theories to bluff innocent people into believing that life comes from chemical reactions. His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda has exposed this bluff in his book Life Comes from Life, which points out that although scientists claim that life comes from chemicals, they cannot produce so much as an insect, even from unlimited quantities of chemicals. Actually, life and consciousness are symptoms of the spirit soul.

    In Life Comes from Life (page 43), Śrīla Prabhupāda has stated, “Living beings move from one bodily form to another. The forms already exist. The living entity simply transfers himself, just as a man transfers himself from one apartment to another. One apartment is first class, another is second class, and another is third class. Suppose a person comes from a lower-class apartment to a first-class apartment. The person is the same. But now, according to his capacity for payment, or karma, he is able to occupy a higher-class apartment. Real evolution does not mean physical development, but development of consciousness.” Within every species of life there is consciousness, and that consciousness is the symptom of the living entity, who is the superior energy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Without understanding this essential point of the transmigration of the conscious living entity throughout 8,400,000 species of life, one cannot possibly understand the words durlabho mānuṣo dehaḥ, “the human body is very rarely achieved.”

    People are now being cheated of this essential understanding. They are completely unaware of the danger of slipping back into the eight million species that lie below the human species. It is natural that a human being think in terms of progress. We want to feel that our life is progressing and that we are advancing and improving the quality of our life. Therefore, it is urgent that people be informed of the great danger of misusing the valuable human life and that they know of the great opportunity the human life affords, the opportunity to take to Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Just as on earth different residential areas are divided into high class, middle class and low class, within the universe there are upper-class, middle-class and lower-class planets. By practice of the yoga system, or by meticulous execution of religious rituals, one can transfer himself to the higher planets within this universe. On the other hand, by neglecting religious principles one will degrade himself to a lower planet. But the Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇa, declares in Bhagavad-gītā (8.16) , ābrahma-bhuvanāl lokāḥ punar āvartino ’rjuna. Thus the final conclusion is that every planet within the material universe is an unsuitable and inappropriate residence, because on each planet there are the primal defects old age and death. The Lord assures us, however, that in His transcendental abode, which lies far beyond the material cosmos, life is everlasting, blissful and absolutely cognizant. The material world is temporary, troublesome and rife with ignorance, but the spiritual world, called Vaikuṇṭha, is eternal, blissful and full of perfect knowledge.

    The highly evolved human brain is a gift given by God so that we may use our intelligence to distinguish between that which is eternal and that which is temporary. As stated in Bhagavad-gītā (2.16) :

    nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ ubhayor api dṛṣṭo ’ntas tv anayos tattva-darśibhiḥ

    “Those who are seers of the truth have concluded that matter has no permanent existence whereas the spirit soul never ceases to exist. Learned seers have concluded this by studying the nature of both.”

    Those who have accepted the Supreme Lord and His abode as the ultimate goal of life are called vaikuṇṭha-priya. Here King Nimi states that to have the personal association of such learned transcendentalists is certainly the perfection of human life. In this connection Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura suggests that we consider the following verse:

    nṛ-deham ādyaṁ su-labhaṁ su-durlabhaṁ plavaṁ su-kalpaṁ guru-karṇadhāram mayānukūlena nabhasvateritaṁ pumān bhavābdhiṁ na taret sa ātma-hā

    “[The Supreme Lord said:] The best of bodies, a human body, is a great attainment, rarely achieved, and may be compared to a boat. The guru is an expert captain for this boat, and I have sent favorable winds (the Vedas ). Thus I have given all facilities for crossing over the ocean of material existence. Any human being who has achieved these excellent facilities of human life but does not cross over the material ocean is to be considered the killer of his own self.” ( Bhāg. 11.20.17 )

    According to Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī, the eternal servants of the Supreme Lord, being controlled by powerful feelings of mercy, descend into the material world as Vaiṣṇavas to deliver the conditioned souls who are bound by the results of their own mundane work. Such Vaiṣṇavas also distribute their mercy to those who are laboriously searching after the impersonal Absolute. Śrī Nārada Muni has stated that without ecstatic love of Godhead such laborious, impersonal contemplation of the Absolute is certainly troublesome ( naiṣkarmyam apy acyuta-bhāva-varjitam ), and what to speak of the innumerable problems of ordinary gross materialistic life. We have practical experience that in the Western countries most people are working hard to get money, laboring under heavenly dreams of sense gratification. Others, having become frustrated with ordinary materialistic life, are trying to negate their personal existence and merge into the existence of God through so-called yoga and meditation. Both classes of unhappy people are receiving the mercy of the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, putting aside their dreams of sense gratification as well as their troublesome impersonal speculation. They are learning to chant the holy names of God, dance in ecstasy, and feast on the holy food offered to the Lord. They become enlivened by the transcendental knowledge spoken by the Lord Himself in the Bhagavad-gītā. As the Lord states in Bhagavad-gītā (9.2) , susukhaṁ kartum avyayam. The actual process of spiritual freedom is joyful to perform and has nothing to do with fruitive activities aimed at sense gratification or with dry impersonal speculation. More and more people are taking to the process of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, becoming joyful, and eagerly distributing Kṛṣṇa’s mercy to others. Thus the whole world will be enlivened and inspired by the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, which is the practical demonstration of the mercy of the Vaiṣṇavas.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    For the conditioned souls, the human body which can be lost at any moment is a rare opportunity for gaining liberation. But I think that even rarer than liberation is the association of devotees who are dear to the Lord. Today, I have seen my good fortune. Human birth is rare for attaining liberation. However meeting the associates of the Lord is rarer, because they bestow bhakti.
